question: Design a URL shortener (like bit.ly).
answer:
Functional: shorten long URL → short code; redirect short → long; optional custom alias, expiry, click analytics.

High-level: API servers → cache (Redis) → DB (SQL or NoSQL). Load balancer in front. CDN optional for redirect edge caching.

ID generation: base62 encode auto-increment ID, or hash (MD5 truncated — collision risk). Store mapping short_code → long_url.

Redirect flow: GET /{code} → cache lookup → 301/302 redirect. Read-heavy — cache aggressively.
tip: 301 = permanent (browser caches, fewer hits); 302 = temporary (better for analytics). Clarify which.
deep:
Requirements & estimates

  • 100M URLs stored, 10:1 read:write ratio.
  • Write: ~100/sec; Read: ~10K/sec peak.
  • Short code: 6–7 base62 chars = 56–62 bits of space.

API design

POST /api/v1/urls   { longUrl, customAlias?, expiry? }  → { shortUrl }
GET  /{shortCode}                                      → 302 redirect

Data model

urls: short_code (PK), long_url, user_id, created_at, expires_at, click_count

ID generation options

ApproachProsCons
Auto-increment + base62No collisions, short codesSingle writer bottleneck; use range allocator per server
Hash (MD5/SHA) truncateDistributedCollisions — must check DB and retry
Pre-generated key poolFast writesOperational overhead

Scaling reads

  • Redis cache-aside for hot codes (80/20 rule).
  • Read replicas if cache miss rate grows.
  • CDN cache 302 responses for viral links (careful with analytics).

Analytics

Don't sync-write click counts — async via Kafka → aggregate in analytics DB. Redirect path stays fast.

How to say it in an interview

"Read-heavy redirect service with rare writes. I'd use base62-encoded IDs from a distributed ID generator, store mappings in SQL with a Redis cache-aside layer, and put a load balancer in front of stateless API servers. Analytics and click counting go async so redirects stay under 100ms."
revise:
**URL shortener**: API → cache (Redis) → DB, behind a load balancer.
• **ID generation** — base62-encode an auto-increment ID (or a truncated hash, with collision handling); redirect on lookup.
• **Interview tip**: **301 = permanent** (browser caches, fewer hits) vs **302 = temporary** (better click analytics) — clarify which they want.

question: Design a notification system (push, email, SMS).
answer:
Functional: send notifications via push/email/SMS; support templates, user preferences, scheduling, delivery status.

Architecture: API receives send request → validate → publish to message queue → channel-specific workers (email worker, push worker, SMS worker) → third-party providers (SendGrid, FCM, Twilio).

Store notification history and user preferences. Use priority queues for OTP vs marketing. Retry with backoff; dead-letter queue for failures.
tip: Never send notifications synchronously in the request path — always queue and return 202 Accepted.
deep:
Requirements

  • 1M notifications/day; bursts during campaigns.
  • Channels: push, email, SMS, in-app.
  • User can opt out per channel and category.
  • OTP: deliver in < 5s; marketing: can be delayed.

Flow

Service → Notification API → Kafka topic(s) → Workers → Provider APIs
                ↓
         Preferences DB + Template store + Delivery log

Key components

  • Template engine — parameterized messages per locale.
  • Preference service — filter before enqueue (don't queue what user opted out of).
  • Rate limiter — per user and per provider to avoid spam flags.
  • Idempotency — dedupe by notification_id to prevent double-send on retry.
  • Scheduler — delayed jobs via scheduled queue or cron scanning due table.

Priority & fan-out

Separate topics: notifications.high (OTP, security) and notifications.low (marketing). High-priority workers scale independently.

Failure handling

  • Provider down → retry 3× with exponential backoff.
  • Permanent failure (invalid email) → mark undeliverable, don't retry.
  • DLQ for manual inspection.

How to say it in an interview

"Async by design — API validates and enqueues, workers handle delivery per channel. I'd check user preferences before enqueue, use priority queues for transactional vs marketing, and track delivery status with idempotent workers so retries don't double-send."
revise:
**Notification system**: API validates → **publish to a queue** → channel-specific workers (email/push/SMS) → providers (SendGrid/FCM/Twilio); store status + respect user preferences.
• **Interview tip**: **never send notifications synchronously** in the request path — **queue and return 202 Accepted**.

question: Design a chat/messaging system (1:1 and group).
answer:
Functional: 1:1 and group chat, message history, online status, read receipts, media attachments.

Real-time: WebSockets (or long polling fallback) between client and chat servers. Use a gateway layer for persistent connections.

Storage: messages in NoSQL/Cassandra (write-heavy, time-ordered) or SQL sharded by conversation_id. Media in object storage (S3).

Delivery: publish message to queue → fan-out to recipient's connected server via pub/sub (Redis). Offline users fetch history on reconnect.
tip: WebSocket connections are stateful — use consistent hashing so a user's socket lands on the same chat server.
deep:
Requirements

  • 50M DAU, 1:1 and groups up to 500 members.
  • Messages delivered in < 500ms when online.
  • Store history; support offline catch-up.

Connection layer

Client ←WebSocket→ Chat Gateway (stateful) ←→ Message Service ←→ DB
                         ↑
                    Redis Pub/Sub (route to correct gateway)

Each user connects to one gateway instance. On message send, service publishes to Redis channel for recipient's gateway.

Message flow (1:1)

  1. Sender POSTs/WebSocket sends message.
  2. Service assigns message_id (snowflake), persists to DB.
  3. Publish to recipient's gateway via pub/sub.
  4. Gateway pushes to recipient's WebSocket.
  5. Sender gets ACK with message_id.

Group chat fan-out

  • Small groups (<50): fan-out on write — write N inbox entries or publish N events.
  • Large groups: fan-out on read — store once, recipients pull on open.

Data model

messages: conversation_id, message_id, sender_id, body, timestamp
conversations: id, type (1:1/group), participants[]
user_inbox: user_id, conversation_id, last_message_at (for chat list)

Presence & read receipts

Online status in Redis with TTL heartbeat. Read cursor per user per conversation. Eventual consistency OK for "last seen".

How to say it in an interview

"Stateful WebSocket gateways for real-time delivery, stateless message service behind them. Persist messages in a write-optimized store sharded by conversation_id. Use pub/sub to route messages to the right gateway. For groups I'd fan-out on write for small groups and fan-out on read for large channels."
revise:
**Chat system**: **WebSockets** (long-poll fallback) via a connection-gateway layer; messages in NoSQL/Cassandra (write-heavy, time-ordered) or SQL sharded by conversation_id; fan-out for groups.
• **Interview tip**: WebSocket connections are **stateful** — use **consistent hashing** so a user's socket lands on the same chat server.

question: Design an e-commerce shopping cart.
answer:
Functional: add/remove items, update quantity, view cart, merge guest → logged-in cart, checkout handoff.

Storage: cart data in Redis (fast, TTL for abandoned carts) keyed by user_id or session_id. Persist to DB on login or checkout.

Inventory: don't hard-reserve on add-to-cart — show availability from inventory service. Reserve stock at checkout with a short TTL lock.

Consistency: cart is per-user/session; eventual consistency OK. Price snapshot at checkout, not on every cart view.
tip: Cart is not an order — keep it lightweight in Redis. The hard part is inventory reservation at checkout.
revise:
**Shopping cart**: store in **Redis** (fast, TTL for abandoned carts) keyed by user/session; persist to DB on login/checkout; **don't hard-reserve inventory on add-to-cart** — reserve at checkout.
• **Interview tip**: **a cart is not an order** — keep it light in Redis; the hard part is **inventory reservation at checkout**.

question: Design a social media news feed (Twitter / Instagram).
answer:
Functional: post content; follow users; view a home feed of posts from people you follow, newest first; like and comment.

The one decision that defines this design: fanout on write vs fanout on read.

  • Fanout on write (push) — when you post, immediately write the post ID into every follower's precomputed feed list (in Redis). Reading a feed is then a single cheap list read. Feeds load instantly. The problem: a celebrity with 50M followers triggers 50M writes for one post.
  • Fanout on read (pull) — store posts once; when a user opens the app, query all the people they follow and merge the results. Cheap writes, but expensive reads on every single feed open.

The real answer is hybrid: fanout on write for normal users (the vast majority, and it makes reads instant), and fanout on read for celebrities above a follower threshold — their posts are merged in at read time. This is what production systems actually do.

Architecture: Post service → Kafka → fanout workers → Redis feed lists per user. Read path: feed service pulls post IDs from Redis, hydrates post content from the post store/cache, merges in celebrity posts, applies ranking, returns a page.
tip: Bring up the celebrity problem yourself before the interviewer does — it's the entire point of this question. 'Pure fanout on write breaks when Virat Kohli posts to 50 million followers' shows you're thinking about the tail, not the average case.
code:
# Fanout on write — precomputed feed per user in Redis
ZADD feed:{userId} {timestamp} {postId}     # sorted set, newest first
ZREVRANGE feed:{userId} 0 49                # read page 1 = one O(log N) call
ZREMRANGEBYRANK feed:{userId} 0 -1001       # cap at 1000 entries

# Hybrid read path
feed  = ZREVRANGE feed:{userId} 0 49             # precomputed (normal users)
celebs = getCelebritiesFollowed(userId)          # small list
extra = fetchRecentPosts(celebs, since=cursor)   # pulled at read time
return rank(merge(feed, extra))[:50]
deep:
Requirements & estimates

  • 500M DAU, each opening the feed ~10×/day → ~58K feed reads/sec average, ~150K peak.
  • ~50M posts/day → ~600 writes/sec. Read:write ≈ 100:1 — this is a read-heavy system, optimise reads.
  • Average 200 followers → fanout on write ≈ 120K feed-list writes/sec. Acceptable. Celebrities are the exception, not the rule.

API design

POST /v1/posts              { text, mediaIds[] }        → { postId }
GET  /v1/feed?cursor=&limit=50                         → { posts[], nextCursor }
POST /v1/users/{id}/follow                             → 204

Use cursor-based pagination, never OFFSET — with a constantly changing feed, offsets duplicate and skip items.

Data model

posts:     post_id (PK), user_id, text, media_ids, created_at
follows:   follower_id, followee_id, created_at    -- PK (follower_id, followee_id)
feed:      Redis ZSET  feed:{user_id} → {score: timestamp, member: post_id}
counters:  Redis  post:{id}:likes  (async-flushed to DB)

Fanout comparison

Fanout on writeFanout on read
Read latencyExcellent (one list read)Poor (N queries + merge)
Write costO(followers) — brutal for celebritiesO(1)
StorageHigh (duplicated per follower)Low
Inactive usersWasted workNo waste

Scaling & refinements

  • Don't fan out to inactive users — skip accounts dormant for 30+ days and build their feed on demand.
  • Cap feed lists at ~1000 entries; older pages fall back to a query.
  • Async everything — fanout, counters, and notifications go through Kafka; the post API returns as soon as the post is durable.
  • Media goes to object storage + CDN, never through the API.
  • Ranking — once you move beyond reverse-chronological, the feed becomes a scoring problem (recency × affinity × engagement), which changes caching because the feed is now personalised per read.

How to say it in an interview

“It's read-heavy at roughly 100:1, so I precompute feeds with fanout on write into Redis sorted sets, which makes a feed read one O(log N) call. That breaks for celebrities, so I use a hybrid: above a follower threshold, posts are pulled and merged at read time. Fanout happens asynchronously through Kafka, I skip inactive users, and I cap each feed list to bound memory.”
revise:
**News feed** — the defining decision is **fanout on write vs read**:
• **Fanout on write (push)** — write the post ID into every follower's precomputed Redis list. **Instant reads**, but a celebrity = 50M writes per post.
• **Fanout on read (pull)** — cheap writes, but merge N followees' posts on **every** feed open.
• **Answer = HYBRID** — fanout on write for normal users, **fanout on read for celebrities** above a follower threshold, merged at read time.
• Redis **ZSET `feed:{userId}`** (score = timestamp), capped at ~1000; fanout async via Kafka; **skip inactive users**; **cursor pagination, never OFFSET**.
• **Interview tip**: raise the **celebrity problem yourself** — it's the whole point.

question: Design a distributed rate limiter.
answer:
Requirements: enforce "N requests per window" per user/API key/IP, across many API servers, with minimal added latency, failing gracefully.

The algorithms, and their trade-offs:

  • Fixed window counter — a counter per key per minute. Trivial and cheap, but has a boundary burst flaw: 100 requests at 11:59:59 and 100 more at 12:00:00 means 200 requests in one second while technically respecting "100/minute".
  • Sliding window log — store a timestamp per request in a sorted set and count entries in the window. Perfectly accurate, but memory grows with request volume.
  • Sliding window counter — weight the previous window's count by how much of it overlaps. Nearly as accurate as the log at fixed memory cost. The usual production choice.
  • Token bucket — tokens refill at a constant rate up to a capacity; each request takes one. Allows controlled bursts, which is usually what you actually want, and it's what most API gateways implement.
  • Leaky bucket — processes at a fixed rate, smoothing output completely. Good for protecting a downstream with a hard throughput ceiling.

Distributed state is the hard part: counters must be shared across all API instances, so they live in Redis, updated with an atomic Lua script (read-modify-write in application code races). Add a small local in-process cache for obviously-over-limit keys to cut Redis calls.
tip: Say what happens when Redis is down — 'fail open' (allow traffic, protect availability) is usually right for a public API; 'fail closed' is right when the limiter guards something expensive or dangerous. Having a considered answer here is what separates a real design from a textbook one.
code:
-- Token bucket in a single atomic Redis Lua script
-- KEYS[1]=bucket key  ARGV: capacity, refillRate, now, requested
local b        = redis.call('HMGET', KEYS[1], 'tokens', 'ts')
local tokens   = tonumber(b[1]) or tonumber(ARGV[1])
local ts       = tonumber(b[2]) or tonumber(ARGV[3])
local elapsed  = math.max(0, tonumber(ARGV[3]) - ts)

tokens = math.min(tonumber(ARGV[1]), tokens + elapsed * tonumber(ARGV[2]))

if tokens < tonumber(ARGV[4]) then
  return {0, tokens}                      -- denied → 429
end

tokens = tokens - tonumber(ARGV[4])
redis.call('HMSET', KEYS[1], 'tokens', tokens, 'ts', ARGV[3])
redis.call('EXPIRE', KEYS[1], 3600)
return {1, tokens}                        -- allowed
deep:
Requirements & estimates

  • 1M active API keys, 100K req/sec peak → the limiter itself must add < 2ms.
  • Redis at ~100K ops/sec per node — shard by key, or use a Redis Cluster.
  • Memory: token bucket stores 2 fields per key ≈ tens of MB for 1M keys. A sliding window log at this volume would be far larger — that's why it loses.

Where to enforce it

LayerGood for
CDN / edge (Cloudflare)Volumetric abuse and DDoS — stops traffic before it costs you anything
API gateway (Kong, Envoy)Per-key and per-tenant quotas. The standard place.
ServiceExpensive-endpoint-specific limits (report generation, exports)

Response contract

HTTP 429 Too Many Requests
Retry-After: 30
X-RateLimit-Limit: 1000
X-RateLimit-Remaining: 0
X-RateLimit-Reset: 1786800000

Always return these headers — a limiter that doesn't tell clients their budget forces them to guess, and they'll guess by retrying hard.

Design details that matter

  • Atomicity — GET-then-SET from app code races under concurrency; use Lua (or INCR with EXPIRE for fixed window).
  • Tiered limits — free vs paid tiers, plus separate limits per endpoint cost class.
  • Failure mode — Redis unavailable → fail open with a local in-memory fallback limit, and alert.
  • Hot keys — one abusive key can hotspot a Redis shard; a local pre-check short-circuits it.

How to say it in an interview

“I'd use token bucket for burst tolerance, implemented as an atomic Lua script in Redis so counters are shared across all API instances. Enforcement sits at the API gateway, with the edge handling volumetric abuse. I return 429 with Retry-After and rate-limit headers, and if Redis is unavailable I fail open with a conservative local limit rather than taking down the API.”
revise:
**Distributed rate limiter** — algorithms:
• **Fixed window** — cheap, but **boundary burst** (2× the limit across the boundary).
• **Sliding window log** — accurate, memory grows with volume.
• **Sliding window counter** — weights the previous window; accurate at fixed memory. **Common production choice.**
• **Token bucket** — refills at a rate, **allows controlled bursts**. What most gateways use.
• **Leaky bucket** — fixed output rate, smooths completely.
• **Distributed state in Redis**, updated by an **atomic Lua script** (GET-then-SET races). Enforce at the **gateway**, edge for DDoS.
• Return **429 + `Retry-After` + `X-RateLimit-*`**.
• **Interview tip**: state the failure mode — **fail open** for a public API, fail closed when guarding something expensive.

question: Design a video streaming platform (YouTube / Netflix).
answer:
Split it in two — the upload/processing pipeline and the playback path. They have completely different characteristics.

Upload & processing (write path, batch, expensive):

  1. Client uploads directly to object storage via presigned multipart URLs — never through your API servers.
  2. Upload completion fires an event onto a queue.
  3. A transcoding pipeline splits the video into chunks and converts each into multiple resolutions and bitrates (240p → 4K) in parallel across a worker fleet. Chunk-level parallelism is what makes a 2-hour film transcode in minutes.
  4. Generate thumbnails, extract metadata, run content moderation, produce subtitles.
  5. Write the manifest (HLS .m3u8 or DASH .mpd) listing every rendition and segment, then publish to the CDN.

Playback (read path, latency-critical, massive scale): the player fetches the manifest, then requests 2–10 second segments over HTTP from the CDN. Adaptive bitrate streaming means the player measures throughput and buffer health and switches rendition per segment — that's why quality drops instead of stalling when your network degrades.

The CDN is the entire scaling story. Video bytes must be served from edge caches close to users; origin only ever sees cache misses. Netflix goes further and places its own appliances inside ISPs.
tip: The insight to lead with: 'video is a solved caching problem, not a compute problem — 99% of the design is getting bytes into a CDN and letting the player adapt'. Then mention that transcoding is chunk-parallel, which is why it's fast.
code:
# HLS manifest — the player picks a rendition, then pulls segments
#EXTM3U
#EXT-X-STREAM-INF:BANDWIDTH=800000,RESOLUTION=640x360
360p/index.m3u8
#EXT-X-STREAM-INF:BANDWIDTH=2500000,RESOLUTION=1280x720
720p/index.m3u8
#EXT-X-STREAM-INF:BANDWIDTH=6000000,RESOLUTION=1920x1080
1080p/index.m3u8

# within 720p/index.m3u8 — segments the player fetches sequentially
#EXTINF:6.0,
seg_00001.ts
#EXTINF:6.0,
seg_00002.ts

# transcoding fanout: chunk-level parallelism
video → split into 6s chunks → N workers × M renditions → reassemble manifests
deep:
Requirements & estimates

  • 500 hours uploaded/minute; 1B hours watched/day.
  • 1080p ≈ 5 Mbps → one hour ≈ 2.25 GB. Storage across ~5 renditions ≈ 4–5× the source.
  • Egress dominates cost — hence CDN offload is a financial requirement, not just a performance one.
  • Read:write is astronomically skewed (~1:10,000+). Optimise ruthlessly for reads.

Data model

videos:    video_id (PK), user_id, title, description, duration,
           status(UPLOADING|PROCESSING|READY|FAILED), created_at
renditions: video_id, resolution, bitrate, codec, manifest_url, size
views:     append-only event stream → batch aggregate (never a synchronous UPDATE)

Key design decisions

  • Segment length — shorter segments adapt faster and reduce live latency, but add request overhead. 4–6s is the common compromise (2s for low-latency live).
  • Storage tiering — hot content on fast storage/CDN; the long tail on cheap cold storage. Most views concentrate on a tiny fraction of the catalogue.
  • Pre-transcode vs on-the-fly — pre-transcode popular renditions; for the long tail, transcode lazily on first request to avoid paying for renditions nobody watches.
  • DRM (Widevine/FairPlay) and signed/expiring CDN URLs for paid content.
  • View counts — never a synchronous DB update per view. Stream to Kafka, aggregate in batches, and deduplicate.

Live streaming differences

Live inverts the constraints: ingest via RTMP/SRT → real-time transcode → short segments → CDN, with a latency budget of seconds. You trade quality-ladder depth for speed, and you can't retry a failed transcode.

How to say it in an interview

“Two pipelines. Upload goes straight to object storage via presigned URLs, then an event-driven transcoding fleet chunks the video and produces a bitrate ladder in parallel, writing HLS/DASH manifests. Playback is pure CDN — the player fetches the manifest and adapts bitrate per segment based on throughput and buffer. Metadata lives in a normal database, and view counts are streamed and aggregated asynchronously.”
revise:
**Video platform = two pipelines.**
• **Upload/processing** — presigned **direct-to-object-storage** upload → event → **transcoding fleet** splits into chunks and produces a **bitrate ladder** (240p–4K) **in parallel** → thumbnails/moderation/subtitles → write **HLS `.m3u8` / DASH** manifest → publish to CDN.
• **Playback** — player fetches the manifest, pulls **4–6s segments over HTTP from the CDN**; **adaptive bitrate** switches rendition per segment using throughput + buffer health (why quality drops instead of stalling).
• **The CDN is the whole scaling story** — origin only sees misses; egress dominates cost.
• Storage tiering for the long tail; **lazy transcode** unpopular renditions; view counts **streamed to Kafka + batch-aggregated**, never a synchronous UPDATE.

question: Design a ride-hailing service (Uber / Ola) — the matching problem.
answer:
Core challenge: millions of drivers broadcasting location every few seconds, and riders needing "find me the nearest available drivers" answered in milliseconds. A naive SELECT ... WHERE distance < 5km over every driver is a full scan — completely unworkable.

The key idea is spatial indexing. Divide the world into cells and index drivers by cell ID, turning a geometric search into a hash lookup:

  • Geohash — encodes lat/long into a string where a shared prefix means spatial proximity. Search = prefix match on the target cell plus its 8 neighbours (you must include neighbours, or you miss drivers just across a cell boundary).
  • Uber's H3 — hexagonal cells; hexagons have uniform distance to all 6 neighbours, unlike squares where diagonal neighbours are farther. Better for radius queries.
  • Redis GEO commands (built on geohash + sorted sets) give you GEOADD/GEOSEARCH out of the box — a pragmatic production answer.

Two separate write paths: driver location updates are extremely high-volume but ephemeral — they go to Redis (in-memory, TTL'd), not to a durable database. Trip state (requested → matched → started → completed → paid) is low-volume but must be durable and transactional.

Matching: find candidate drivers in nearby cells → filter by availability, vehicle type, rating → rank by ETA (road-network time, not straight-line distance) → offer to the best driver with a short timeout → fall through to the next on decline.
tip: Two details that land: (1) rank by ETA, not euclidean distance — a driver 500m away across a river is useless; (2) location updates are ephemeral and belong in Redis, not Postgres. Writing 1M locations/sec to a durable DB is the classic wrong answer.
code:
# Driver location: high-volume, ephemeral → Redis GEO
GEOADD drivers:available 72.8777 19.0760 "driver_8821"
EXPIRE drivers:available 30                # stale drivers fall out

# Rider request: nearest available drivers within 3 km
GEOSEARCH drivers:available
  FROMLONLAT 72.8800 19.0750
  BYRADIUS 3 km ASC COUNT 20 WITHDIST

# Geohash: shared prefix = spatial proximity
# te7ud  ≈ 5 km cell   |  te7udd ≈ 1.2 km cell  |  te7uddq ≈ 150 m cell
# ALWAYS query the target cell + its 8 neighbours (boundary problem)

# Trip state: low-volume, durable, transactional → Postgres
UPDATE trips SET status='MATCHED', driver_id=:d
 WHERE trip_id=:t AND status='REQUESTED';   -- optimistic, prevents double-match
deep:
Requirements & estimates

  • 1M active drivers, location update every 4s → 250K writes/sec. This alone rules out a durable DB for locations.
  • 100K ride requests/minute → ~1,700 matches/sec.
  • Matching latency budget: < 1 second end to end.

Services

Location Service   ← driver pings → Redis GEO (ephemeral, TTL)
Matching Service   → spatial query → filter → ETA rank → dispatch offer
Trip Service       → durable state machine (Postgres), the source of truth
Pricing Service    → surge = f(demand/supply per cell, time)
Notification/WS    → live driver tracking to the rider's app
ETA Service        → road-network routing, not straight-line distance

The concurrency problem

Two riders must never be matched to the same driver. Solutions: a short-lived distributed lock on the driver ID during dispatch, plus an optimistic status check in the trip update (WHERE status='REQUESTED') so a double-assignment fails at the database rather than being silently accepted. Offers must expire (10–15s) so a non-responsive driver doesn't block the rider.

Surge pricing

Computed per geographic cell as a function of open requests vs available drivers over a rolling window. It's a streaming aggregation (Kafka + windowed counts), and the price must be locked at quote time so the rider is charged what they were shown.

Live tracking

WebSocket (or long-lived connection) from the matched driver's app → server → rider's app. Only push during an active trip; broadcasting all driver positions to all riders doesn't scale.

How to say it in an interview

“Driver locations are high-volume and ephemeral, so they live in Redis GEO with a TTL — a geohash/H3 cell index turns proximity search into a hash lookup instead of a scan. Matching queries nearby cells, filters by availability, ranks by ETA from the road network, and dispatches with a short offer timeout. Trip state is a durable state machine in Postgres, and I guard against double-matching with a lock plus a conditional status update.”
revise:
**Ride-hailing / matching**:
• **Spatial indexing** turns proximity search into a hash lookup — **geohash** (shared prefix = nearby; **always query the cell + 8 neighbours** for the boundary problem), **H3 hexagons** (uniform neighbour distance), or **Redis GEO** (`GEOADD`/`GEOSEARCH`).
• **Two write paths**: driver locations are **high-volume + ephemeral → Redis with TTL** (250K writes/sec would destroy a durable DB); **trip state is durable + transactional → Postgres**.
• **Matching**: nearby cells → filter (available, vehicle, rating) → **rank by ETA on the road network, not straight-line distance** → offer with a **10–15s timeout** → next driver on decline.
• **No double-match**: distributed lock on driver + **conditional update** (`WHERE status='REQUESTED'`).
• **Surge** = demand/supply per cell (streaming aggregation), **price locked at quote time**.

question: Design a payment system. How do you guarantee you never double-charge?
answer:
Payments are where correctness beats availability. Two absolute rules: never double-charge, and never lose money — the books must always balance.

Idempotency is the core mechanism. The client generates an Idempotency-Key for each payment intent. The server stores it with the result in a table with a unique constraint. A retry with the same key returns the original stored response instead of charging again. Retries are inevitable — the client times out, the network drops, the user double-taps — so the design must assume duplicates rather than hope they don't happen.

Double-entry ledger — model money movement as immutable ledger entries where every transaction has balanced debits and credits summing to zero. Never UPDATE balance SET ...; balance is derived from the ledger. This gives you a complete audit trail and makes reconciliation possible — you can always prove where money went.

State machine: INITIATED → AUTHORIZED → CAPTURED → SETTLED, with FAILED and REFUNDED branches. Transitions are explicit and only ever move forward — never mutate a payment record in place.

The unavoidable reality: the payment gateway is an external system you can't transact with atomically. If your DB commit succeeds but the gateway call times out, you don't know whether the charge happened. Resolve it with the gateway's own idempotency key plus a reconciliation job that compares your ledger against the provider's settlement file daily and flags every mismatch.
tip: The follow-up is always 'what if the gateway times out — did the charge go through?'. The correct answer is: you can't know synchronously. You pass an idempotency key to the gateway so a retry is safe, mark the payment PENDING, and let reconciliation resolve it. Anyone claiming certainty here hasn't built payments.
code:
-- Idempotency: the unique constraint IS the guarantee
CREATE TABLE payment_requests (
  idempotency_key TEXT PRIMARY KEY,          -- duplicate insert → conflict
  user_id         TEXT NOT NULL,
  amount_minor    BIGINT NOT NULL,           -- integer paise/cents, NEVER float
  currency        CHAR(3) NOT NULL,
  status          TEXT NOT NULL,
  response_body   JSONB,
  created_at      TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT now()
);

-- Retry-safe: second call returns the stored response, no second charge
INSERT INTO payment_requests (idempotency_key, user_id, amount_minor, currency, status)
VALUES (:key, :user, :amount, 'INR', 'INITIATED')
ON CONFLICT (idempotency_key) DO NOTHING
RETURNING *;

-- Double-entry ledger: every transaction sums to ZERO
CREATE TABLE ledger_entries (
  entry_id    BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  txn_id      UUID NOT NULL,
  account_id  TEXT NOT NULL,
  direction   TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (direction IN ('DEBIT','CREDIT')),
  amount_minor BIGINT NOT NULL CHECK (amount_minor > 0),
  created_at  TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT now()
);
-- invariant, assert continuously:
-- SELECT txn_id FROM ledger_entries GROUP BY txn_id
--   HAVING SUM(CASE WHEN direction='DEBIT' THEN amount_minor ELSE -amount_minor END) <> 0;
deep:
Money representation

Store amounts as integers in the minor unit (paise, cents) with an explicit currency code. Floating point for money is a genuine bug: 0.1 + 0.2 != 0.3. Never use FLOAT/DOUBLE; integers or DECIMAL only.

The flow

1. Client → POST /payments  (Idempotency-Key: uuid)
2. Insert payment_request (unique key) → if conflict, return stored result
3. Write ledger entries + status INITIATED in ONE local transaction
4. Call gateway WITH the same idempotency key
5. Gateway webhook (or poll) → AUTHORIZED / FAILED → append ledger entries
6. Capture → SETTLED; daily reconciliation against the provider's file

Webhooks are hostile input

  • Verify the signature — anyone can POST to your webhook URL.
  • Expect duplicates and out-of-order delivery — process idempotently, keyed on the provider's event ID.
  • Never trust the amount in the webhook alone — verify against your own record.
  • Return 200 fast and process asynchronously, or the provider will retry and pile on.

Reconciliation

A daily job pulls the provider's settlement report and compares it line by line with your ledger. Any mismatch — charged but not recorded, recorded but not charged, amount differs — raises an alert for manual review. This is not optional; it's how you catch the failures the happy path can't.

How to say it in an interview

“Every payment carries a client-generated idempotency key stored under a unique constraint, so retries return the original result instead of charging twice. Money moves as immutable double-entry ledger entries — balance is derived, never updated in place — and amounts are integers in the minor unit. Since the gateway can't participate in my transaction, I pass the idempotency key through, treat webhooks as untrusted and duplicate-prone, and run daily reconciliation against the provider's settlement file.”
revise:
**Payment system** — never double-charge, never lose money.
• **Idempotency key** per payment, stored under a **UNIQUE constraint**; a retry returns the **stored response**, no second charge. Retries are inevitable — design for duplicates.
• **Double-entry ledger** — immutable entries, debits + credits **sum to zero**; balance is **derived**, never `UPDATE balance`. Gives audit trail + reconciliation.
• **State machine**: INITIATED → AUTHORIZED → CAPTURED → SETTLED (+ FAILED/REFUNDED), forward-only.
• **Money = integers in the minor unit** (paise/cents) — **never float**.
• **Gateway can't join your transaction** — pass the idempotency key through, mark PENDING, and resolve via **daily reconciliation** against the settlement file.
• **Webhooks**: verify signature, expect **duplicates + out-of-order**, process idempotently.

question: Design a ticket booking system (BookMyShow / IRCTC). How do you prevent overselling?
answer:
The whole problem is concurrency on scarce inventory: 50,000 people trying to book 100 seats in the same second, and you must sell each seat exactly once.

The two-phase model — hold then confirm:

  1. Hold/lock — when a user selects seats, atomically mark them HELD with a short expiry (5–10 minutes) before sending them to payment. This is what stops two users paying for the same seat.
  2. Confirm — on successful payment, transition HELD → BOOKED.
  3. Expire — a background job (or Redis TTL) releases holds that were never confirmed, returning seats to inventory.

Preventing overselling — the mechanisms:

  • Conditional update (optimistic) — UPDATE seats SET status='HELD' WHERE seat_id=? AND status='AVAILABLE'. If it updates 0 rows, someone else won. Simple, no lock held, and the database enforces correctness.
  • Pessimistic lock — SELECT ... FOR UPDATE for multi-seat atomicity (all seats or none). Correct, but locks reduce throughput under heavy contention.
  • Unique constraint on (event_id, seat_id) in the bookings table — the ultimate backstop; even if application logic is wrong, the database refuses a duplicate.

Never check-then-write in application code (if (available) { book() }) — that's a textbook race condition. The atomicity must live in the database or in an atomic Redis operation.
tip: For a flash sale, add a virtual waiting room / queue in front — admitting users at a controlled rate turns a 50,000-way race into a manageable stream and protects the database. Mentioning that unprompted shows you've thought past the happy path.
code:
-- Optimistic hold: atomic, no lock held, DB enforces correctness
UPDATE seats
   SET status = 'HELD', held_by = :userId, held_until = now() + interval '8 minutes'
 WHERE seat_id = ANY(:seatIds)
   AND show_id = :showId
   AND (status = 'AVAILABLE'
        OR (status = 'HELD' AND held_until < now()));   -- reclaim expired holds
-- rows_updated < seatIds.length  →  someone else got one → fail the whole request

-- Multi-seat atomicity, deterministic order to avoid deadlocks
BEGIN;
  SELECT * FROM seats
   WHERE seat_id = ANY(:seatIds) AND show_id = :showId
   ORDER BY seat_id                 -- consistent order prevents deadlock
     FOR UPDATE;
  -- verify all AVAILABLE, then update
COMMIT;

-- Final backstop: the DB cannot be talked into overselling
ALTER TABLE bookings ADD CONSTRAINT uq_seat_per_show UNIQUE (show_id, seat_id);

-- General admission (no seat map): atomic counter
DECRBY tickets:show_991:remaining 2      -- Redis; if result < 0, roll back
deep:
Requirements & estimates

  • Normal load is trivial; the design is entirely dictated by the flash-sale spike — a popular concert can draw 100K concurrent users for 10K seats.
  • Read:write is extremely skewed — most users are browsing seat maps, only a fraction book. Cache the seat map aggressively; never cache the booking decision.

Data model

events:   event_id, name, venue_id, starts_at
shows:    show_id, event_id, screen_id, show_time
seats:    seat_id, show_id, row, number, price,
          status(AVAILABLE|HELD|BOOKED), held_by, held_until, version
bookings: booking_id, user_id, show_id, seat_ids[], amount,
          status(PENDING|CONFIRMED|CANCELLED), UNIQUE(show_id, seat_id) via join table

Handling the spike

  • Virtual waiting room — queue users at the edge and admit N/sec. Turns a stampede into a stream.
  • Read replicas + cache for seat availability display (accept that it's slightly stale — the hold is the source of truth).
  • Shard by show_id — contention is naturally partitioned per show, so hot shows don't affect others.
  • Reject early — if inventory is exhausted, fail at the edge rather than letting requests reach the database.

The stale-seat-map problem

A user sees a seat as available (cached), tries to book, and it's gone. This is unavoidable and must be handled as a UX problem, not prevented: return a clear "that seat was just taken, here are alternatives" and refresh the map. Trying to make the seat map perfectly consistent for 100K viewers would destroy throughput.

Payment interaction

The hold must outlive the payment flow but not by much. If payment succeeds after the hold expired and the seat was resold, you must refund automatically and surface it clearly — so hold duration should comfortably exceed the payment gateway's timeout.

How to say it in an interview

“Two-phase: an atomic conditional update places a time-limited hold before payment, and a background job reclaims expired holds. Overselling is prevented in the database — a conditional update that affects zero rows means you lost the race, with a unique constraint as the final backstop — never a check-then-write in application code. For flash sales I add a waiting room to control admission, shard by show, and treat a stale seat map as a UX problem rather than trying to make it strongly consistent.”
revise:
**Ticket booking** — the problem is **concurrency on scarce inventory**.
• **Two-phase: HOLD then CONFIRM** — atomically mark seats `HELD` with a **5–10 min expiry BEFORE payment**; confirm on success; a background job/TTL **reclaims expired holds**.
• **Prevent overselling in the DB**: **conditional update** (`WHERE status='AVAILABLE'` → 0 rows = you lost), **`SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`** for multi-seat atomicity (**order by seat_id** to avoid deadlocks), and a **UNIQUE(show_id, seat_id)** backstop.
• **NEVER check-then-write in app code** (`if (available) { book() }`) — textbook race condition.
• **Flash sale**: **virtual waiting room** admitting N/sec, shard by `show_id`, reject early at the edge.
• Stale seat map is a **UX problem**, not a consistency problem — show 'just taken, try these'.

question: Design a file storage and sync service (Dropbox / Google Drive).
answer:
Functional: upload/download files, sync across a user's devices, share with others, version history, offline edits.

The central technique is chunking with content-addressed storage. Split each file into fixed or content-defined blocks (~4 MB), hash each block (SHA-256), and store blocks in object storage keyed by their hash. Metadata records the ordered list of block hashes that make up a file version. This one decision gives you four things at once:

  • Delta sync — editing one paragraph of a 500 MB file re-uploads only the changed blocks, not the file.
  • Deduplication — identical blocks are stored once, globally. The same PDF shared by 10,000 users costs one copy.
  • Resumable uploads — a failed transfer resumes at the block level.
  • Cheap versioning — a new version is just a new block list, sharing unchanged blocks with the old one.

Split metadata from data. The metadata service (files, versions, block lists, permissions, sharing) is a small, transactional, strongly consistent database. The block store is object storage — huge, immutable, and dumb. They scale completely differently.

Sync: each device holds a cursor/version vector. On change, the client uploads new blocks, commits a new version in metadata, and the server notifies other devices (long-poll or WebSocket). Those devices diff their local block list against the server's and download only what's missing.
tip: Content-addressed chunking is the answer to this entire question — say it early. 'Blocks keyed by their own hash' simultaneously solves delta sync, dedupe, resumability, and versioning, and that's why every product in this space works this way.
code:
# A file version is just an ordered list of block hashes
file: report.pdf  v7
blocks: [
  "sha256:a3f9...",   # unchanged from v6 → not re-uploaded
  "sha256:c71b...",   # unchanged
  "sha256:9e04...",   # CHANGED → only this block uploads
  "sha256:2d88..."    # unchanged
]

# Upload negotiation: ask what's missing before sending anything
POST /v1/blocks/check  { hashes: [...] }
→ { missing: ["sha256:9e04..."] }        # dedupe across ALL users
PUT  /v1/blocks/sha256:9e04...           # upload only the missing block
POST /v1/files/{id}/commit { version: 7, blocks: [...] }

# Sync: client polls/subscribes with its cursor
GET /v1/delta?cursor=8821
→ { changes: [{ path, versionId, blocks[], deleted }], cursor: 8905 }
deep:
Data model

users:        user_id, email, quota_bytes, used_bytes
files:        file_id, owner_id, path, current_version, is_deleted, updated_at
versions:     version_id, file_id, size, block_hashes[], created_by, created_at
blocks:       hash (PK), size, refcount, storage_url     -- immutable, dedup'd
shares:       file_id, shared_with_user_id, permission(VIEW|EDIT)
devices:      device_id, user_id, last_cursor, last_seen

Conflict resolution

Two devices edit the same file offline. Options: last-write-wins (simple, silently loses data — usually unacceptable), keep both as "conflicted copy" (what Dropbox does — safe and honest), or CRDTs/OT for genuinely collaborative editing (what Google Docs does — far more complex, only worth it for real-time co-editing). Choose based on whether the product is file sync or collaborative editing.

Garbage collection

Blocks are shared, so you can't delete a block when one file referencing it is deleted. Maintain a refcount, or run a periodic mark-and-sweep over the metadata. Deleting a referenced block is silent, unrecoverable data corruption — this deserves care and a safety delay.

Other decisions worth naming

  • Client-side encryption breaks cross-user dedupe (identical files encrypt differently under different keys). Convergent encryption is a workaround with known privacy trade-offs — a real tension worth acknowledging.
  • Content-defined chunking (rolling hash) beats fixed-size when bytes are inserted: fixed-size blocks all shift and every block changes; content-defined boundaries stay stable.
  • Notifications — long-poll or WebSocket per device; fall back to periodic polling for reliability.

How to say it in an interview

“I'd chunk files into content-addressed blocks stored in object storage, with a separate transactional metadata service holding the ordered block list per version. That gives delta sync, global dedupe, resumable upload, and versioning from one mechanism. Devices sync via a cursor and download only missing blocks. Conflicts create a conflicted copy rather than silently losing an edit, and blocks are garbage-collected by refcount.”
revise:
**File storage & sync** — the core technique is **chunking + content-addressed storage**: split files into ~4MB blocks, **key each block by its SHA-256 hash**.
That single decision gives: **delta sync** (only changed blocks upload), **global dedupe**, **resumable uploads**, and **cheap versioning** (a version = a new block list sharing old blocks).
• **Split metadata from data** — small transactional metadata DB (files, versions, block lists, permissions) vs huge dumb immutable **object storage** for blocks.
• **Sync** via a per-device **cursor**; server notifies (WebSocket/long-poll), client downloads only missing blocks.
• **Conflicts** — last-write-wins loses data; **conflicted copy** is the honest default; CRDT/OT only for real-time co-editing.
• Blocks are shared → **refcount / mark-and-sweep GC** before deleting.

question: Design a web crawler.
answer:
Functional: start from seed URLs, fetch pages, extract links, follow them, store content — at billions of pages, without being blocked or trapped.

The loop: URL frontier → fetcher → parser → link extractor → dedupe → back into the frontier. The interesting engineering is in everything that makes that loop not break.

  • URL frontier — a prioritised queue, but with a hard constraint: politeness. You must not hammer one domain with 1,000 parallel requests. Standard design is per-host queues with a rate limit per host, plus priority queues so important pages are crawled more often.
  • Deduplication — at billions of URLs, a hash set doesn't fit in memory. Use a Bloom filter ("definitely not seen" is free) backed by a persistent store for verification.
  • Content dedupe — the same content appears at many URLs. Hash the normalised content, or use SimHash for near-duplicate detection.
  • Crawler traps — infinite calendars, session IDs in URLs, and dynamically generated infinite depth. Defend with max depth, per-domain page caps, URL normalisation, and pattern detection.
  • robots.txt and crawl-delay must be respected and cached per host.

Architecture: stateless fetcher workers pulling from a distributed queue (Kafka), with the frontier and seen-set in a shared store. Fetchers are I/O-bound, so use async I/O with high concurrency rather than thread-per-request.
tip: Politeness is what interviewers are checking for. A candidate who designs a fast crawler without per-host rate limiting has designed a denial-of-service tool that will get its IPs banned within an hour.
code:
# Frontier: per-host queues enforce politeness, priority drives order
frontier = {
  "example.com":  { queue: [...], nextFetchAt: t+1.0s, crawlDelay: 1.0 },
  "wikipedia.org":{ queue: [...], nextFetchAt: t+0.5s, crawlDelay: 0.5 }
}

# Worker loop
while true:
  host = pickHostWhereNextFetchAt <= now()      # ready + highest priority
  url  = frontier[host].queue.pop()
  if not robots.allows(host, url): continue

  page = fetch(url, timeout=10s)                # async I/O, not a thread each
  frontier[host].nextFetchAt = now() + crawlDelay

  if seen.mightContain(contentHash(page)): continue   # Bloom filter
  store(page)

  for link in extractLinks(page):
    link = normalise(link)                      # strip fragments, sort params,
    if depth(link) > MAX_DEPTH: continue        # lowercase host, drop session IDs
    if not urlSeen.mightContain(link):
      frontier[hostOf(link)].queue.push(link)

# Normalisation matters — these are ONE page:
#   http://Example.com/a?b=1&c=2#frag
#   http://example.com/a?c=2&b=1
deep:
Requirements & estimates

  • 1B pages/month → ~400 pages/sec sustained. Average page ~500 KB → ~200 MB/sec ingest, ~500 TB/month raw (compress it).
  • URL seen-set at 10B URLs: a hash set is far too large for memory; a Bloom filter at 1% FP ≈ 12 GB. This is the canonical Bloom filter use case.
  • Fetchers are I/O-bound — one machine can hold thousands of concurrent connections with async I/O.

Components

Seed URLs → URL Frontier (Kafka + per-host scheduling)
          → Fetcher workers (async, respect robots.txt + crawl-delay)
          → Parser (extract text, links, metadata)
          → Dedupe (Bloom filter for URLs, SimHash for content)
          → Storage (object storage for raw HTML, index for extracted text)
          → back to Frontier

Politeness & prioritisation

ConcernMechanism
Don't overload a hostPer-host queue + crawl-delay; only one in-flight request per host
Crawl important pages morePriority by PageRank-ish score, freshness, update frequency
Recrawl policyAdaptive — news sites hourly, static pages monthly
Identify yourselfHonest User-Agent with a contact URL

Failure handling

  • Timeouts, 5xx → retry with backoff, then give up and record the failure.
  • Redirect chains → cap the depth, and record the final URL for dedupe.
  • Worker dies mid-page → at-least-once delivery from the queue means pages may be fetched twice; storage must be idempotent (key by URL hash).

How to say it in an interview

“It's a distributed producer-consumer loop: a URL frontier feeds stateless async fetchers, which parse, dedupe, store, and push new links back. The two hard parts are politeness — per-host queues with crawl-delay so I don't DoS anyone — and dedupe at scale, where I use a Bloom filter for seen URLs and SimHash for near-duplicate content. Traps are handled with depth limits, per-domain caps, and URL normalisation.”
revise:
**Web crawler** — loop: **frontier → fetcher → parser → link extraction → dedupe → frontier**.
• **Politeness is the key requirement** — **per-host queues + crawl-delay**, one in-flight request per host, respect **robots.txt**. Without it you've built a DoS tool and get banned.
• **Dedupe at scale** — a hash set of 10B URLs doesn't fit in memory → **Bloom filter** (~12 GB @ 1% FP); **SimHash** for near-duplicate *content*.
• **URL normalisation** (sort params, strip fragments/session IDs, lowercase host) — many URLs are one page.
• **Crawler traps** (infinite calendars, generated depth) → max depth, per-domain caps, pattern detection.
• Fetchers are **I/O-bound** → async I/O with high concurrency, not thread-per-request. Storage must be **idempotent** (at-least-once queue).

question: Design a distributed cache (like Redis / Memcached).
answer:
Requirements: sub-millisecond GET/SET, scale beyond one machine's memory, survive node failure, and evict sensibly when full.

Data distribution — consistent hashing with virtual nodes, so adding or removing a node remaps only K/N keys instead of invalidating the entire cache. Clients can compute the target node themselves (client-side sharding, no extra hop) or go through a proxy (simpler clients, one more hop).

Eviction policy — the cache is bounded, so something must go when it's full:

  • LRU — evict least recently used. Good general default; implemented as a hash map + doubly linked list for O(1) get and put.
  • LFU — evict least frequently used. Better when a stable hot set exists; resists a one-off scan flushing your working set.
  • TTL-based — expire by age. Usually combined with LRU.
  • Random — surprisingly acceptable and very cheap.

Replication & failure — each shard has a primary and one or more replicas. Async replication keeps writes fast but can lose recent writes on failover; that's usually acceptable for a cache, since the source of truth is the database. Failover is automatic via a monitor (Redis Sentinel or Cluster).

Memory management — the real engineering. Slab allocation (Memcached) avoids fragmentation; expiry is done lazily on access plus a background sampler, because actively scanning every key for expiry would be O(n) and destroy latency.
tip: The design detail worth volunteering: expired keys are removed lazily on read plus by a random background sampler — not by scanning. Eagerly expiring millions of keys would block the single-threaded event loop, which is exactly the kind of trade-off interviewers want to hear you reason about.
deep:
Design decisions and their trade-offs

DecisionOptionsTrade-off
ShardingClient-side vs proxyClient = fewer hops, fatter clients; proxy = simpler clients, extra latency + a component to run
ThreadingSingle-threaded event loop (Redis) vs multi-threaded (Memcached)Single-threaded gives atomicity for free and no lock contention, but one slow command (KEYS *) blocks everything
PersistenceNone / snapshot / append-only logA pure cache needs none; persistence turns it into a datastore with different durability guarantees
ConsistencyAsync replicationFast writes, possible loss on failover — acceptable because the DB is the source of truth

Cache patterns the client uses

  • Cache-aside (lazy loading) — app checks cache, on miss reads the DB and populates. Most common; only requested data is cached.
  • Write-through — write to cache and DB together. Cache is never stale, writes are slower.
  • Write-behind — write to cache, flush to DB asynchronously. Fast writes, risk of loss.
  • Read-through — the cache itself loads from the DB on miss.

Operational hazards to mention

  • Hot key saturating one shard → local client-side cache in front, or replicate the key.
  • Big keys — a single 500 MB value blocks the event loop on serialisation and skews shard memory.
  • Stampede on expiry → jittered TTLs and single-flight loading.
  • Never run KEYS * in production — it's O(n) and blocks; use SCAN.

How to say it in an interview

“Consistent hashing with virtual nodes distributes keys so a node change remaps only K/N of them. Each shard has a primary and async replicas with automatic failover — losing a few recent writes is fine because the database is the source of truth. Eviction is LRU or LFU implemented in O(1), expiry is lazy plus background sampling to avoid blocking, and clients use cache-aside with jittered TTLs to prevent stampedes.”
revise:
**Distributed cache**:
• **Distribution** — **consistent hashing + virtual nodes** (a node change remaps only **K/N** keys). Client-side sharding (no extra hop) vs proxy (simpler clients).
• **Eviction** — **LRU** (hash map + doubly linked list = O(1)) is the default; **LFU** resists a one-off scan flushing the hot set; TTL usually combined with LRU.
• **Replication** — primary + async replicas, automatic failover; losing recent writes is **acceptable for a cache** because the DB is the source of truth.
• **Expiry is LAZY** (on access) **+ background sampling** — actively scanning all keys would block the single-threaded event loop.
• Patterns: **cache-aside** (most common), write-through, write-behind, read-through.
• Hazards: **hot keys**, **big keys**, stampede on expiry (**jitter TTLs**), and **never `KEYS *`** in prod — use `SCAN`.

question: Design a distributed job scheduler (cron at scale).
answer:
Functional: schedule jobs (one-off at a time, or recurring by cron expression), execute them reliably across a worker fleet, retry failures, and never run a job twice when you said once.

Two-layer design — separate deciding what should run from running it:

  • Scheduler — periodically scans for jobs whose next_run_at has passed and enqueues them. Must be highly available but must not double-enqueue.
  • Workers — stateless consumers pulling from the queue, executing, and reporting status. Scale horizontally with load.

The hard problems:

  1. Don't run twice. If two scheduler instances scan simultaneously, both enqueue the same job. Fix with leader election (only the leader schedules — simple, but the leader is a bottleneck) or, better, an atomic conditional claim: UPDATE ... SET status='CLAIMED' WHERE status='PENDING' AND next_run_at <= now(), letting the database arbitrate.
  2. Don't lose jobs. A worker that dies mid-execution must not silently drop the job. Use visibility timeouts (SQS-style) or a heartbeat + lease, so an unacknowledged job returns to the queue.
  3. At-least-once is the realistic guarantee, so jobs must be idempotent. Exactly-once across a network and a crash boundary isn't achievable; idempotency is how you make at-least-once behave like exactly-once.
  4. Scanning at scale — SELECT * WHERE next_run_at <= now() over 100M rows every second doesn't work. Use a time-bucketed index or a priority queue keyed by execution time (Redis sorted set scored by timestamp).
tip: The line that matters: 'exactly-once execution is not achievable, so I make jobs idempotent and aim for at-least-once with deduplication'. Candidates who promise exactly-once are describing something that doesn't exist across process crashes.
code:
-- Atomic claim: the DB arbitrates, no leader needed
UPDATE jobs
   SET status = 'RUNNING',
       claimed_by = :workerId,
       lease_until = now() + interval '5 minutes',
       attempts = attempts + 1
 WHERE job_id IN (
   SELECT job_id FROM jobs
    WHERE status = 'PENDING' AND next_run_at <= now()
    ORDER BY next_run_at
    LIMIT 100
    FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED          -- workers don't block each other
 )
RETURNING *;

-- Reclaim jobs from dead workers (expired lease)
UPDATE jobs SET status='PENDING', claimed_by=NULL
 WHERE status='RUNNING' AND lease_until < now();

-- Time-bucketed scheduling in Redis: O(log N), no table scan
ZADD jobs:due {epochSeconds} {jobId}
ZRANGEBYSCORE jobs:due -inf {now} LIMIT 0 100

-- After a successful recurring run, compute the next occurrence
UPDATE jobs SET status='PENDING', next_run_at = :nextFromCron WHERE job_id = :id;
deep:
Data model

jobs:      job_id, name, type, payload, cron_expr, next_run_at,
           status(PENDING|RUNNING|SUCCEEDED|FAILED), attempts, max_attempts,
           claimed_by, lease_until, timeout_sec, priority
runs:      run_id, job_id, started_at, finished_at, status, error, worker_id
           -- append-only history for observability and debugging

Failure semantics

FailureHandling
Job throwsRetry with exponential backoff up to max_attempts, then dead-letter
Worker crashesLease expires → job returns to PENDING → another worker picks it up
Job hangstimeout_sec enforced by the worker; lease expiry as the backstop
Previous run still goingOverlap policy: skip, queue, or allow concurrent — must be explicit per job
Scheduler down for an hourCatch-up policy: run all missed occurrences, or only the latest

Details people forget

  • Time zones and DST — "2:30am daily" happens twice on one day a year and not at all on another. Store the timezone with the cron expression and use a library; do not hand-roll this.
  • Thundering herd at midnight — everyone writes 0 0 * * *, so a huge spike hits at 00:00. Add jitter, or spread jobs across the window.
  • Priority + fairness — one tenant scheduling 100K jobs must not starve everyone else. Use per-tenant queues or weighted fair queuing.
  • Observability — alert on jobs that didn't run, not just ones that failed. A silent scheduler is the failure mode nobody notices.

How to say it in an interview

“I separate scheduling from execution. A time-indexed store (Redis sorted set or a bucketed index) finds due jobs without scanning, and workers claim them atomically with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED plus a lease — so a dead worker's job is reclaimed automatically. Execution is at-least-once, so jobs are idempotent with a dedupe key. Retries use exponential backoff into a dead-letter queue, and I alert on jobs that didn't run, not just failures.”
revise:
**Distributed job scheduler** — separate **deciding what runs** (scheduler) from **running it** (stateless workers).
• **Don't run twice**: leader election (simple, bottleneck) or better an **atomic claim** — `UPDATE ... WHERE status='PENDING'` with **`FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`** so the DB arbitrates and workers don't block.
• **Don't lose jobs**: **lease/visibility timeout + heartbeat**; expired lease → job returns to PENDING.
• **At-least-once is the real guarantee → jobs MUST be idempotent.** Exactly-once across a crash boundary doesn't exist.
• **Don't scan** 100M rows — use a **time-bucketed index / Redis ZSET scored by timestamp** (`ZRANGEBYSCORE`).
• Forgotten details: **time zones + DST**, **midnight thundering herd** (`0 0 * * *` → add jitter), overlap policy, catch-up policy, per-tenant fairness.
• **Alert on jobs that DIDN'T run**, not only failures.

question: Design an autocomplete / typeahead system.
answer:
The defining constraint is latency: suggestions must appear within ~100ms of a keystroke, and every keystroke is a request. A user typing "laptop" generates 6 requests. At scale that's more QPS than the main search itself.

Data structure — a trie (prefix tree): each node is a character, and the path from the root spells a prefix. The critical optimisation is to precompute and store the top-K completions at every node. Then a lookup is: walk the prefix (O(length of prefix), tiny) and return the stored list — no traversal of the subtree, no sorting at query time.

Ranking — suggestions are ordered by a score combining frequency, recency (trending queries should surface fast), personalisation, and often geography.

The build path is separate and offline. Query logs stream into an aggregation pipeline that computes frequencies over a rolling window, builds a new trie, and publishes it. Serving nodes load the prebuilt trie into memory. You never mutate the serving trie per query — updates are periodic full or incremental rebuilds, because a read-only in-memory structure is what makes sub-10ms responses possible.

Client-side matters as much as the backend: debounce input (~50ms) so you don't fire a request per keystroke, cache results per prefix locally, and cancel in-flight requests when the user keeps typing.
tip: Say 'store the top-K at each node so the query is a prefix walk with no sorting' — that's the whole trick. Then add the client-side debounce, because halving your QPS with three lines of frontend code is the cheapest optimisation available.
deep:
Requirements & estimates

  • 10M searches/day, ~5 keystrokes each → ~50M suggest requests/day, ~600/sec average and far higher at peak. Autocomplete QPS exceeds search QPS — this is the point people miss.
  • p99 latency budget < 100ms including network, so server time must be single-digit milliseconds.
  • 10M unique queries in a trie with top-5 per node fits comfortably in memory on each serving node — which is why this can be a read-only in-memory service.

Scaling the trie

  • Replicate, don't shard, if it fits. A fully in-memory read-only trie replicated across many stateless nodes is simpler and faster than sharding.
  • If it doesn't fit — shard by prefix (all "a*" on one set of nodes). Beware skew: prefixes aren't uniformly distributed.
  • Cache the hottest prefixes at the CDN/edge — short prefixes like "a" or "la" are requested enormously more often than long ones, and their results change slowly.

Update strategy

ApproachFreshnessCost
Full rebuild (hourly/daily)LagsSimple, safe, atomic swap
Incremental mergeMinutesMore complex, needs care under concurrency
Real-time overlaySecondsSmall hot layer for trending, merged at query time

A common production shape is a stable rebuilt trie plus a small real-time overlay for trending queries — breaking news needs to appear in minutes, not tomorrow.

Extras worth mentioning

  • Typo tolerance — edit distance is expensive at query time; precompute common misspellings or use n-gram matching as a fallback.
  • Filtering — offensive or sensitive queries must be blocklisted; this is a real product requirement, not an afterthought.
  • Personalisation — merge a small per-user history layer with the global list at query time.

How to say it in an interview

“A trie with the top-K completions precomputed at every node, held read-only in memory and replicated across stateless serving nodes — so a query is just a prefix walk with no sorting, returning in single-digit milliseconds. The trie is built offline from query logs with frequency and recency scoring, published periodically with an atomic swap, plus a small real-time overlay for trending. On the client I debounce, cancel in-flight requests, and cache per prefix, which cuts QPS dramatically.”
revise:
**Autocomplete/typeahead** — the constraint is **latency (~100ms per keystroke)**, and **suggest QPS exceeds search QPS** (5 keystrokes per search).
• **Trie with the top-K completions PRECOMPUTED at every node** → a query is a **prefix walk with no sorting**, single-digit ms.
• **Serving trie is read-only in memory, replicated** across stateless nodes (simpler and faster than sharding). Shard by prefix only if it doesn't fit.
• **Build offline**: query logs → Kafka → windowed frequency + recency scoring → build trie → publish with an **atomic swap**. Add a small **real-time overlay** for trending.
• **Client-side is half the win**: **debounce ~50ms**, **cancel in-flight requests**, cache per prefix. Edge-cache short hot prefixes.
• Extras: typo tolerance via precomputed misspellings/n-grams, blocklist filtering, personalisation layer.

question: Design a real-time leaderboard and counting system.
answer:
Requirements: millions of players, scores updating constantly, and queries for "top 100" plus "my rank" — both in milliseconds.

Why the obvious approach fails: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM scores WHERE score > :myScore to compute a rank is O(n) per query. At 10M rows and thousands of QPS, the database dies.

The answer is a Redis sorted set (ZSET), which is built for exactly this — a skip list plus hash map giving O(log N) insert and rank lookup:

  • ZADD to update a score — O(log N).
  • ZREVRANGE 0 99 WITHSCORES for the top 100 — O(log N + 100).
  • ZREVRANK for "my rank" — O(log N). This is the operation that's impossible to do cheaply in SQL.

Scaling beyond one node: a single ZSET with 100M entries is large and hot. Options: shard by score range and merge (complex), bucket by time window (daily/weekly leaderboards are naturally smaller and are what users actually care about), or approximate deep ranks — return exact ranks for the top N and an estimated percentile for everyone else. Most players only care whether they're top 10 or roughly "top 5%".

Durability: Redis is the serving layer, not the source of truth. Score events go to Kafka → durable store for audit and rebuild, and the ZSET can be reconstructed from that log.
tip: The '“my rank” is O(log N) in a ZSET but O(n) in SQL' point is the crux of this question. Also mention that for 100M players you approximate ranks outside the top N — exact rank #4,271,908 is expensive to compute and nobody needs it.
code:
# Update a score — O(log N)
ZADD leaderboard:global 15200 "player_8821"
ZINCRBY leaderboard:global 150 "player_8821"     # relative update

# Top 100 — O(log N + 100)
ZREVRANGE leaderboard:global 0 99 WITHSCORES

# "My rank" — O(log N). This is what SQL can't do cheaply.
ZREVRANK leaderboard:global "player_8821"        # → 4271 (0-indexed)
ZSCORE   leaderboard:global "player_8821"

# Players around me (the leaderboard slice users actually want)
rank = ZREVRANK leaderboard:global "player_8821"
ZREVRANGE leaderboard:global (rank-5) (rank+5) WITHSCORES

# Time-bucketed boards: smaller, hotter, and what users care about
ZADD leaderboard:2026-08-05 15200 "player_8821"
EXPIRE leaderboard:2026-08-05 604800

# High-cardinality unique counting — HyperLogLog, ~12KB for billions
PFADD  daily:uniques:2026-08-05 "player_8821"
PFCOUNT daily:uniques:2026-08-05        # ~0.81% standard error
deep:
Requirements & estimates

  • 100M registered players, 10M daily active, ~5 score updates each → ~600 writes/sec average, much higher during events.
  • Leaderboard reads far exceed writes — everyone checks their rank.
  • ZSET memory: roughly 100 bytes per entry → 10M players ≈ 1 GB. Fine on one node; 100M is where you shard or bucket.

Architecture

Game/App → score event → Kafka (durable log, source of truth)
                          ├→ Redis ZSET  (serving layer, O(log N) reads)
                          └→ Warehouse   (analytics, audit, rebuild source)

Writing to Redis and the durable store from application code is a dual write — prefer publishing the event and having consumers update both, so Redis can always be rebuilt from the log.

Counting at scale — pick the right structure

NeedStructureCost
Exact countINCR counterExact, tiny
Ranked setSorted set (ZSET)O(log N), ~100B/entry
Unique visitorsHyperLogLog~12 KB for billions, 0.81% error
Top-K heavy hittersCount-Min SketchSub-linear, approximate
MembershipBloom filterSpace-efficient, false positives

Choosing an approximate structure where exactness isn't required is the difference between 12 KB and many GB.

Consistency and fairness

  • Ties — ZSET orders equal scores lexicographically by member; if you need "earlier achiever ranks higher", encode the timestamp into the score (e.g. score * 10^10 - timestamp).
  • Cheating — validate score submissions server-side; a leaderboard is a magnet for tampering.
  • Hot key — one global ZSET is a single hot key; replicas serve reads, and time/region bucketing spreads load.

How to say it in an interview

“A Redis sorted set, because it gives O(log N) score updates, top-N reads, and rank lookup — that last one is what makes SQL unworkable, since computing a rank there is a full count. Scores flow through Kafka so Redis stays a rebuildable serving layer rather than the source of truth. For very large boards I bucket by time window and return exact ranks only for the top N, approximating percentile below that, and I use HyperLogLog for unique counts.”
revise:
**Real-time leaderboard** — SQL fails because computing a rank (`COUNT(*) WHERE score > mine`) is **O(n) per query**.
• **Redis sorted set (ZSET)** — skip list + hash map: **`ZADD`** O(log N), **`ZREVRANGE 0 99`** for the top N, and **`ZREVRANK`** for **'my rank' in O(log N)** — the operation SQL can't do cheaply.
• **Scale**: bucket by **time window** (daily/weekly boards are smaller and what users care about), shard by score range, or **approximate ranks outside the top N** (nobody needs exact rank #4,271,908).
• **Durability** — Redis is the **serving layer, not the source of truth**; score events go to **Kafka** so the ZSET can be rebuilt.
• **Approximate structures**: **HyperLogLog** for uniques (~12KB for billions, 0.81% error), Count-Min Sketch for top-K, Bloom filter for membership.
• Ties: encode the timestamp into the score. Validate scores **server-side** (cheating).

question: Design a centralised logging and metrics pipeline.
answer:
Requirements: collect logs and metrics from thousands of hosts/containers, make them searchable within seconds, retain them affordably, and — critically — never let the observability system take down the applications it observes.

The pipeline: collect → buffer → process → store → query.

  1. Collect — a lightweight agent per node (Fluent Bit, Vector, OTel Collector) tailing container stdout. It must be resource-capped, because an agent that OOMs the node has caused an outage.
  2. Buffer — Kafka in the middle. This is the single most important design decision: it decouples producers from consumers, absorbs traffic spikes, and lets the storage layer go down for maintenance without losing a single log line. Without a buffer, a slow Elasticsearch backs pressure all the way into your applications.
  3. Process — parse, enrich (add pod/service/region metadata), redact PII, sample, and route by class.
  4. Store — different data, different stores: logs to Elasticsearch or Loki, metrics to Prometheus/Mimir (time-series), traces to Tempo/Jaeger. One store cannot serve all three well.
  5. Query — Grafana or Kibana over all of them, correlated by trace ID.

Tiered retention is what makes it affordable: hot and searchable for 7–14 days, then compressed in object storage for the compliance tail.
tip: The principle to state up front: 'the observability pipeline must fail independently of the applications it monitors'. Agents drop or spill to disk rather than block, Kafka absorbs backpressure, and a full Elasticsearch must never make the checkout service slow.
code:
# Pipeline
[app stdout] → Fluent Bit/Vector (per node, resource-capped)
             → Kafka (buffer, replay, decoupling)   ← the key component
             → stream processors (parse, enrich, redact, sample, route)
             ├→ Elasticsearch / Loki   (logs,    7-14d hot)
             ├→ Prometheus / Mimir     (metrics, downsampled long-term)
             ├→ Tempo / Jaeger         (traces,  tail-sampled)
             └→ S3 / Glacier           (raw archive, compliance)

# Agent config: never let the agent hurt the node
[SERVICE]
    Mem_Buf_Limit     50MB          # cap memory
    storage.type      filesystem    # spill to disk instead of blocking
    storage.max_chunks_up 128

[FILTER]                            # drop noise BEFORE it costs anything
    Name    grep
    Match   kube.*
    Exclude log (GET /health|GET /ready|GET /metrics)

[OUTPUT]
    Name    kafka
    Match   kube.*
    Retry_Limit  5                  # then drop — do NOT block the app
deep:
Requirements & estimates

  • 5,000 containers × 100 log lines/sec × 500 bytes ≈ 250 MB/sec ≈ 21 TB/day raw. Compression (~10:1) and sampling are not optional.
  • Metrics: 5,000 targets × 500 series × 1 sample/15s ≈ 165K samples/sec.
  • Query latency target: seconds for recent data, minutes acceptable for archive.

Why Kafka in the middle

Without a bufferWith Kafka
ES slow → agents block → apps slowES slow → Kafka lag grows → apps unaffected
ES down → logs lostES down → replay from Kafka when it returns
Traffic spike → dropped dataSpike absorbed by retention
One consumerMany consumers, independently paced

Cost and volume control

  • Drop at the agent — health checks, probe traffic, framework startup noise. Filtering at the source is free; filtering after ingestion is not.
  • Sample — keep 100% of ERROR and slow requests, sample INFO/DEBUG.
  • Tiered retention — hot 7–14 days, then S3/Glacier.
  • Downsample metrics — full resolution 15 days, 5-minute rollups for a year.
  • Watch cardinality — one unbounded metric label can dominate the entire bill.

Multi-tenancy

In a shared platform, one noisy team must not degrade everyone: per-tenant quotas and rate limits at ingestion, separate indices/streams per tenant, and per-tenant cost attribution so the bill lands with the team generating the volume.

How to say it in an interview

“Agent per node, Kafka as the buffer, stream processors for parsing and enrichment, then purpose-built stores — Loki or Elasticsearch for logs, a TSDB for metrics, Tempo for traces — with Grafana querying across all three correlated by trace ID. Kafka is the critical piece: it decouples producers from consumers so a slow or down storage layer never applies backpressure to the applications. Cost is controlled by dropping noise at the agent, sampling, and tiered retention.”
revise:
**Logging/metrics pipeline**: **collect → buffer → process → store → query**.
• **Agent per node** (Fluent Bit/Vector/OTel), **resource-capped** — an agent that OOMs the node causes an outage.
• **Kafka as the buffer is THE key decision** — decouples producers from consumers, absorbs spikes, allows storage downtime with **replay**. Without it, a slow Elasticsearch **backpressures into your apps**.
• **Purpose-built stores**: logs → Loki/Elasticsearch, metrics → Prometheus/Mimir, traces → Tempo/Jaeger. One store can't serve all three.
• **Cost control**: drop noise **at the agent** (free), sample (keep 100% of errors), **tiered retention** (7–14d hot → object storage), **downsample metrics**, watch **cardinality**.
• **Interview tip**: **'the observability pipeline must fail independently of the apps it monitors.'**
